meta.name: Microsoft Azure Data Engineer Associate DP-203
meta.notes: [new pack: 12 authored DP-203 questions covering data storage design, data processing, data security, and optimization; answer positions balanced 3/3/3/3] [scheduled-agent]

questions.question: You are loading a multi-terabyte sales fact table into a dedicated SQL pool in Azure Synapse Analytics. The table is almost always joined to large dimension tables on CustomerKey. Which table design minimizes data movement during those joins?
options: Replicate the table to every Compute node
Create the table as a heap with no clustered index
questions.explanation: Hash distribution on the join column (CustomerKey) co-locates matching rows on the same distribution, so joins on that key run without shuffling data between nodes. Round-robin spreads rows evenly but forces data movement on joins. Replicated tables are meant for small dimensions (roughly under 2 GB), not multi-terabyte facts. Heap versus clustered index controls storage and indexing, not distribution, so it does not address join data movement.

questions.question: A 50 MB product dimension table in a dedicated SQL pool is joined to many large fact tables. You want each Compute node to hold a full local copy so joins avoid shuffling the table at query time. Which distribution should you choose?
questions.explanation: A replicated table stores a full copy on every Compute node, eliminating data movement for joins with small dimension tables (recommended for tables under about 2 GB). Hash and round-robin distributions split rows across distributions, so the table must be moved or shuffled at join time. Partitioning controls how rows are grouped for pruning and maintenance; it does not place a full copy on each node.

questions.question: You are provisioning an Azure Storage account that will serve as a data lake for Azure Synapse and Databricks, and you need directory-level POSIX ACLs plus atomic directory operations. Which option must you enable?
options: The hierarchical namespace (Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2)
questions.explanation: Enabling the hierarchical namespace turns a general-purpose v2 account into Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, which adds true directories, atomic directory operations, and POSIX-style ACLs. GRS is a replication and redundancy setting. Soft delete protects against accidental deletion but adds no directory semantics. NFS 3.0 is a separate access protocol and is not what provides ACLs and directory structure for analytics.

questions.question: Queries against a large Parquet dataset in your data lake almost always filter by date. How should you organize the files so that a serverless SQL pool reads only the relevant data?
options: Store every file in a single flat container
Compress all files into one large ZIP archive per year
Name files sequentially (file001, file002, ...) with no folders
Store files in date-based folder partitions such as /year=2026/month=05/day=29/
questions.explanation: Partitioning the lake into date-based folders lets the engine apply partition elimination (pruning) using filepath() predicates, so only folders matching the date filter are scanned. A single flat container or sequential file names force a full scan. A ZIP archive is not a splittable analytical format and must be fully read and decompressed, defeating pruning.

questions.question: You need a file format for large analytical tables in the data lake that stores data by column, compresses well, and supports predicate and column pushdown for Spark and serverless SQL queries. Which format best fits?
questions.explanation: Parquet is a columnar, compressed, self-describing format that supports column pruning and predicate pushdown, making it ideal for analytical queries in Spark and Synapse serverless SQL. JSON and CSV are row-oriented text formats that must be parsed in full and lack column statistics, so they scan far more data. Plain text logs are unstructured and even less efficient for analytics.

questions.question: You want to run ad-hoc T-SQL queries directly over Parquet files in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 without provisioning or paying for a running cluster, and be billed per terabyte of data processed. Which Azure Synapse capability should you use?
options: The built-in serverless SQL pool with OPENROWSET
questions.explanation: The serverless SQL pool requires no provisioned infrastructure, is billed per terabyte of data processed, and queries files in the lake directly using OPENROWSET (or external tables). A dedicated SQL pool reserves and bills compute (DWUs) whether or not it is queried. A Spark pool uses notebooks and Spark, not pay-per-query T-SQL over files. Azure Analysis Services is a separate tabular modeling engine, not a lake query service.

questions.question: An Azure Data Factory pipeline must copy only rows inserted or changed since the previous run from a SQL source. Which approach implements this incremental load?
options: Always run a full copy and let the sink deduplicate
Store a high-watermark value (such as max LastModified) and copy only rows greater than the stored watermark
Use a tumbling window of one second on the source
Disable the staging area on the Copy activity
questions.explanation: The watermark pattern records the last processed value (such as the maximum LastModified or an incrementing key), then each run copies only rows greater than that stored value and updates the watermark afterward. A full copy every run is not incremental and wastes resources. Tumbling windows schedule pipeline runs but do not by themselves filter changed rows. The staging setting affects PolyBase/COPY staging, not change detection.

questions.question: In an Azure Stream Analytics job you must report the event count for each fixed, non-overlapping 30-second interval, with every event belonging to exactly one window. Which windowing function should you use?
questions.explanation: A tumbling window divides time into fixed-length, contiguous, non-overlapping segments, so each event falls into exactly one window, which is ideal for counting events per 30 seconds. Hopping windows can overlap, so an event may appear in several. Sliding windows produce output as events enter or leave and overlap continuously. Session windows group bursts of activity separated by gaps, so their length varies.

questions.question: In Azure Databricks you must incrementally ingest new files as they land in a Data Lake Storage Gen2 folder, processing only files not seen before and without re-listing the entire directory each run. Which feature is designed for this?
options: Auto Loader (the cloudFiles source in Structured Streaming)
A static batch read with spark.read.parquet over the whole folder
The COPY INTO command run as a one-time full load
Manually deleting files after each successful read
questions.explanation: Auto Loader uses the cloudFiles source to incrementally and efficiently process new files as they arrive, tracking processed files through checkpoints (and optional file notifications) so it never reprocesses or fully re-lists the directory. A static spark.read reprocesses everything each run. A single COPY INTO is a one-time bulk load, not continuous incremental ingestion. Deleting source files is destructive and loses the raw data.

questions.question: Support staff must see customer email addresses with most characters hidden (for example aXXX@XXXX.com) while the underlying stored values stay unchanged and privileged roles still see full data. Which Azure SQL or Synapse feature provides this?
questions.explanation: Dynamic Data Masking obfuscates data in query results for non-privileged users while leaving the stored values intact; members with the unmask permission still see full values. TDE encrypts data at rest on disk and is transparent to queries, so it does not mask results. Always Encrypted protects data end-to-end with client-side keys, hiding it even from admins, which is more than required. Row-Level Security filters which rows a user sees, not how column values are displayed.

questions.question: In a dedicated SQL pool, each regional manager must see only the sales rows for their own region, enforced automatically inside the database regardless of how the query is written. Which feature should you implement?
options: Row-Level Security using a security predicate function and a security policy
Dynamic Data Masking on the Region column
Granting SELECT on separate per-region views only
questions.explanation: Row-Level Security uses an inline table-valued predicate function bound to the table through a security policy, so the engine transparently filters rows (for example by region) for every query without changing application code. Column-level security restricts which columns, not which rows, are visible. Dynamic Data Masking only obscures displayed values. Per-region views can work but are not automatic, scale poorly, and are easy to bypass if base-table access is granted.

questions.question: An Azure Data Factory pipeline must authenticate to Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 without storing any account keys, secrets, or connection strings in the linked service. What is the recommended approach?
options: Embed the storage account key directly in the linked service
Generate a long-lived SAS token and paste it into the pipeline
Store the account key in the pipeline parameters
Use the data factory's managed identity and grant it the Storage Blob Data Contributor role
questions.explanation: A system-assigned or user-assigned managed identity lets Data Factory authenticate to Storage through Microsoft Entra ID with no secrets in the configuration; you grant it an RBAC role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor on the account or container. Embedding the account key or storing it in parameters exposes a powerful long-lived secret. A long-lived SAS token is still a secret that must be rotated and can leak, so it is not the recommended secret-free option.
